say: Your phone knows exactly where you are. But here's the weird part. It never sends a single thing to space. It just listens.
About thirty GPS satellites circle the Earth, twenty thousand kilometers up. Each one loops the whole planet twice a day.
And every satellite keeps shouting just two things. Where it is, and the exact time it sent that message.
That signal flies at the speed of light, but it still takes a tiny moment to reach you. Measure the delay, and you know the distance.
One satellite puts you somewhere on a giant bubble. Add two more, and the bubbles overlap in just one spot. That's you.
But your phone's clock is pretty cheap, so a fourth satellite fixes its timing. That's why GPS needs at least four.
Timing is everything. Light moves about thirty centimeters in a billionth of a second, so tiny clock errors mean big map errors.
Now it gets weirder. Einstein says speed slows time, but weaker gravity speeds it up. So satellite clocks gain thirty eight microseconds a day.
Sounds tiny, right? But left alone, your location would drift about ten kilometers a day. So engineers set the clocks slow before launch.
